text_blocks.snippet: Social anxiety disorder (SAD), also known as social phobia, is a persistent and excessive fear of social situations where one might be judged, scrutinized, or embarrassed by others. This fear can significantly interfere with daily life, impacting work, school, relationships, and overall well-being. Individuals with SAD may experience intense anxiety before, during, and after social events, worrying about potential negative outcomes and feeling self-conscious.
snippet_highlighted_words: a persistent and excessive fear of social situations where one might be judged, scrutinized, or embarrassed by others

text_blocks.snippet: Key characteristics of Social Anxiety Disorder:

list.title: Intense fear of social situations:
list.snippet: This fear can be specific to certain situations (like public speaking) or encompass a wide range of social interactions.

list.title: Avoidance:
list.snippet: Individuals with SAD may avoid social situations to minimize anxiety, leading to isolation and missed opportunities.

list.title: Physical symptoms:
list.snippet: Physical manifestations of anxiety, such as blushing, trembling, sweating, nausea, and difficulty talking, are common.

list.title: Negative self-perception:
list.snippet: Individuals with SAD often have low self-esteem and engage in negative self-talk.

list.title: Impact on daily life:
list.snippet: Social anxiety can interfere with work performance, academic achievement, and the ability to form and maintain relationships.

list.title: Duration:
list.snippet: To be diagnosed with SAD, the symptoms must persist for at least six months.

list.title: Comorbidity:
list.snippet: SAD can co-occur with other mental health conditions, such as generalized anxiety disorder, panic disorder, and depression.

list.title: Potential for severe impairment:
list.snippet: In some cases, social anxiety can be severe, leading to significant limitations in social, occupational, and academic functioning.
